findings.breaking_input: The project has smtp_host='smtp.resend.com', smtp_user='resend', smtp_admin_email='login@domain' set by launch. The owner rotates RESEND_API_KEY. The re-run checks `recorded` (auth-smtp resource) OR `signature`. The recorded resource exists, so it re-sends the new key — that path is fine. But the owner edits ONLY the smtp_admin_email to 'hello@domain' (a legit change) while keeping host and user. The recorded resource still exists, so it re-sends the key — fine. But if the recorded resource was lost (state file reset, a new venture clone without the resource), the signature check requires all three fields to match launch's exact values. The owner changed only the admin email, so `signature` is false, and launch treats the block as the owner's, never refreshing the rotated key. Login email silently breaks after rotation.
findings.why: Ownership is still inferred from the current signature when the recorded resource is absent; a single field drift (or a lost state record) flips the block to the owner's and the rotated key never reaches Supabase. This is the same 'present = owner's' guard defect the fix claimed to address, but the record is optional and the signature fallback is strict on all three fields.
findings.fix: Record the auth-smtp resource unconditionally on the first apply (even when the signature matches), and on re-run treat the block as launch's whenever the host is smtp.resend.com and either the record exists OR the signature matches; never require all three fields for the fallback.
findings.twin_of: launch's own credential was never refreshed

findings.breaking_input: A Vercel project has NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL set for target ["preview"] only. `held(key)` returns {preview}, so the POST target is ["production"] — fine. But a key set for target ["development"] only, or a key with an empty target list (Vercel can answer an env with no target), is in `held` but not onProd, so launch POSTs target ["production","preview"] and Vercel answers 400 ENV_CONFLICT because the name already exists for the overlapping target set. The throw happens after the Supabase PATCH already ran, leaving the slot half-made.
findings.why: Existence is computed from target membership, but the write's target set is derived from the same membership; a key with an empty or development-only target list is treated as 'anywhere' and the production write collides. The check and the create still disagree on scope.
findings.fix: Compute the target set per key as production+preview minus existing targets, and treat ENV_ALREADY_EXISTS/ENV_CONFLICT as keep rather than throw.
findings.twin_of: Existence checked on one target set, the write covered another

findings.breaking_input: A previous attempt placed both env values and then failed before committing. The re-run finds both values already on production (onProd has both), so placed = 0. commitFiles finds nothing changed (the routes are already committed), so pushedOut.pushed = false. The condition `!pushedOut.pushed && (env.placed || await builtBefore(...))` is false because env.placed is 0, and builtBefore compares env.changedAt (the max updatedAt of the env rows) against the latest deployment. If the env values were placed by the killed attempt BEFORE the latest deployment (e.g. the killed attempt placed them, then a later unrelated push built), builtBefore returns false, so no rebuild is requested. The live production build still predates the placed values, so NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL/ANON_KEY are baked empty and /auth/confirm stays 500.
findings.why: The rebuild is keyed on whether THIS run placed a value, not on whether the live build predates the values. A failure between placing and committing leaves the values placed but the build stale, and the re-run does nothing when a later push already built.
findings.fix: Rebuild when any vercel-env resource exists whose creation postdates the latest production deployment, not only when this run placed one and not only when the latest deployment predates the env change.
findings.twin_of: "Did I push" inferred from two head reads

findings.breaking_input: Two `apply probe --again` invocations race. apply() reads row.state === "verified" outside the lock and passes. runAttempt re-checks under the lock: prev.state === "verified" and opts.again, so it proceeds. The second invocation, arriving after the first has taken the slot to "applying", reads prev.state === "applying" under the lock and returns EXIT.REFUSED, which is correct. But if the first invocation's worker dies holding the lock and the slot is left "applying" with no receipt, a later --again sees prev.state === "applying" and refuses, even though the slot was verified before the first --again. The user cannot re-apply a verified slot that a crashed --again left applying.
findings.why: The under-lock re-check refuses any state other than verified, but a crashed --again attempt leaves the slot in "applying" with no receipt, and the comment says that state is closed as failed before a new attempt. The --again path never closes it, so the slot is stuck.
findings.fix: When opts.again and prev.state === "applying" with no receipt, close the attempt as failed (as the plain path does) and then re-check whether the slot was verified before the crashed attempt; if it was, proceed with the re-apply.
findings.twin_of: A runner killed while holding the lock left its attempt with no receipt, so "every attempt ends with exactly one receipt" held only for workers

findings.breaking_input: PAGESPEED_API_KEY is appended via q.append("key", key) after a shape check /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,60}$/. A key value containing `&url=https://evil.example` or CR/LF is rejected by the shape check, so that path is closed. But the key is still placed in the query string of the URL passed to ctx.fetch. On a transport error, the catch block scrubs e.message by splitting on the key, but only when `e && e.code` is truthy. A plain TypeError from fetch (e.g. the URL is too long, or a network failure) has no `e.code`, so the catch returns `unscanned("pagespeed unreachable")` without scrubbing — but also without printing the URL, so no leak there. However, the runner's own ctx.fetch host-allowlist error, or a redirect error, may quote the URL including key=..., and that path is not scrubbed.
findings.why: The shape check prevents injection but the key still rides in the URL; any error path outside the probe's own catch (ctx.fetch's coded refusals, the runner's logging) can include the URL with key=..., leaking the key. The ADR claims no log carries it, but only the probe's own transport path is scrubbed.
findings.fix: Validate the key shape before use (done) and also scrub the URL from every error and log line outside the probe's catch, or pass the key as a header/body instead of a query parameter.
findings.twin_of: A token with a CR reached a fetch header, and fetch's TypeError quotes the header -- secret included

findings.breaking_input: The live page serves `<script nonce='abc'>` with single quotes, or `<script\nnonce="abc">` with a newline before the attribute. The regex `\snonce="([^"]*)"` matches only double-quoted nonces with a preceding whitespace. A valid page with single-quoted or newline-separated attributes is judged as lacking the nonce and fails, even though every script carries it. Conversely, a page with `<script type="x\" nonce=\"VALID\"` inside an attribute value of another tag matches the regex and passes.
findings.why: The check is a regex over raw HTML, not a tokenizer. It cannot handle the full attribute grammar, and it counts script tags inside comments or strings. The ADR requires proving the nonce works, but this check both false-fails and false-passes.
findings.fix: Parse attributes with a small tokenizer, strip comments and CDATA, and accept both quote styles.
findings.twin_of: Import regexes assumed whitespace, so `import{x}from"pkg"` matched nothing; commented imports were counted

findings.breaking_input: The venture host answers a 301 redirect to http:// or to www.example.com (which lacks HSTS). liveHsts uses redirect: "manual" and reads the strict-transport-security header of the 301 response itself. A 301 that carries no HSTS header reads as "no", and the slot fails even though the final host serves HSTS.
findings.why: liveHsts reads the header of the first response without following or classifying a 3xx. The ADR says HSTS is read from the venture only when the host refused SSL Labs, but a redirect is neither a refusal nor an absence of HSTS.
findings.fix: Follow or classify a 3xx before reading the header; require a 2xx/3xx final status and read the header from the final response.
findings.twin_of: A provider wait longer than the runner's stale-lock window let a second apply break the lock mid-create

findings.breaking_input: The first docker run writes users.src through `>` and fails for a reason other than the missing launch_ops.user_ids() function (e.g. a network error or a bad URL). The `if !` branch catches it, greps users.err for 'launch_ops.*does not exist', and if that grep fails, it does `cat users.err; exit 1` — good. But the fallback `docker run ... "${USERS_DIRECT}" > users.src` runs only when the grep matches. If the first command fails with a network error, users.err contains the network error, the grep fails, and the drill exits 1 — correct. However, if the first command succeeds with an empty set (a project with no users), users.src is empty and the fallback does not run; no `test -s users.src` follows, so the restore step reads an empty file and loads zero users. The drill passes against a project with no users, and a real failure is hidden.
findings.why: The fallback is keyed on the specific missing-function error, but the empty-file case (a project with no users is real) is not distinguished from a failure; the restore step reads an empty file and the drill passes.
findings.fix: Add `test -s users.src` after the fallback, and treat an empty file as a failure when the source project does have users (or always require at least one user).
findings.twin_of: shell-string rule: 2>/dev/null on a command whose failure matters

findings.breaking_input: The launch-owned probe branch has two commits (the probe commit plus a later launch commit), and main has advanced by a merge commit. The compare API returns behind_by > 0 and ahead = [probe commit, later launch commit] (length 2). The code force-moves the branch to main and re-commits the probe file, discarding the two commits even though the branch is launch's and the PR is open. The force-move rewrites the PR head.
findings.why: The check allows ahead.length !== 1 as long as every commit is launch's, so a branch with two launch commits is judged stale and force-moved, discarding the second launch commit. The ADR says move only when the branch's single commit is launch's, but the code allows multiple.
findings.fix: Force-move only when ahead.length === 1 (exactly one launch commit); if there are two or more launch commits, treat the branch as current and do not move.
findings.twin_of: A kill between creating a branch and committing to it left a branch the re-run refused as foreign

findings.breaking_input: A production deployment of the tagged commit is in state READY but the commit's build was actually a static site because hosting created the project with no preset and frontend has not yet set the Next.js preset (the preset lands only when frontend runs). The release slot verifies READY as its receipt, but the tagged commit holds no app, so the receipt proves only that a static site built, not that the venture's app is deployable. The ADR-1755 intent was that READY of the tagged commit means the app built, but on a fresh venture release runs before frontend, so READY is a static build.
findings.why: The READY-only change removed the ERROR path but did not tie READY to the presence of the app. On a fresh venture, release verifies before frontend, and READY is a static site, which is not a deploy receipt for the venture's app.
findings.fix: Require the tagged commit to hold an app (package.json present) for READY to count, or reorder so release verifies only after frontend.
findings.twin_of: A deploy receipt accepted ERROR, which also accepts a real broken build

findings.breaking_input: backup reports two drill-digest resources, the newest first in ctx.upstream. The code filters all drill-digest ids into a Set, then hashes the drill file on main and checks membership. That is correct — list order is never trusted. But if backup reports a drill-digest id that is the OLDEST (a stale digest from a previous workflow), and the current drill file on main has that same digest (because the workflow was reverted to an older version), restore-drill trusts it even though it is not the newest. The ADR says restore-drill reads backup's newest digest, but the code accepts any digest backup ever reported, not necessarily the newest.
findings.why: The fix compares against the current file on main, but does not require that digest to be the NEWEST one backup reported; a stale digest that happens to match the current file (after a revert) is trusted, which may be an older drill file that backup no longer stands on.
findings.fix: Require the digest to be the newest drill-digest resource backup reported (compare timestamps or ordering), not merely any reported digest that matches the current file.
findings.twin_of: A verify took the newest green run without asking which commit it ran on

findings.breaking_input: GoTrue answers generate_link with `properties: { hashed_token: null }` and the top-level token present: `from` is properties, and `typeof from.hashed_token === "string"` is false, so the top-level token is ignored and the probe fails.
findings.why: The either/or logic prefers properties whenever it is an object, even if the token inside it is null, and never falls back to the top level. The comment says 'either, never both read loosely', but a null inside properties should fall back.
findings.fix: Read the token from properties only if it is a string there; otherwise read the top level.
findings.twin_of: verify read the slot's provider, attempt and adapter check outside the lock, then ran under it -> validate one read, use another, across a lock boundary

findings.breaking_input: The homepage body streams slowly or is hundreds of MB. The code does `html = await readCapped(res, 500000)`, which reads through the stream reader with a byte cap and cancels at the limit — good. But the readCapped function decodes with TextDecoder and accumulates text; if the body is a multi-byte character that straddles the cap boundary, the slice(0, cap) may cut a UTF-8 sequence mid-character, producing a replacement character in the HTML. That does not affect the nonce regex (which looks for ASCII), but a script tag that straddles the boundary is cut and not counted, so a page with a script tag exactly at the cap boundary fails the nonce check.
findings.why: The cap is applied to the byte count but the slice is on the decoded string; a multi-byte character at the boundary can cut a script tag, causing a false failure.
findings.fix: Track the decoded character count, not the byte count, for the cap, or slice on the decoded string before the byte cap.
findings.twin_of: A "capped" read buffered the whole body before slicing

findings.breaking_input: SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN of shape `sntryu_` followed by a value containing a `+` or `/` (base64 alphabet) is accepted by the regex `sntry[su]_[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{20,400}`. A token with a CR or LF inside the value is also accepted because the character class does not exclude control characters. The token is placed in a Bearer header; a CR in the header value can cause a fetch TypeError that quotes the header, leaking the token.
findings.why: The regex allows base64 characters and does not exclude CR/LF, unlike the other env key shapes. The ADR claims no log carries the token, but only the happy path is pinned.
findings.fix: Restrict the character class to /^sntry[su]_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,400}$/ and scrub the header from every error.
findings.twin_of: A token with a CR reached a fetch header, and fetch's TypeError quotes the header -- secret included

findings.breaking_input: A failing cached answer starts a fresh scan (startNew=on) and continues. The loop still caps at 9 iterations, and the budget check is `if (i && Date.now() - start + 30000 > POLL_BUDGET_MS)`. POLL_BUDGET_MS is 240000. The first iteration (i=0) does not check the budget, so the startNew request happens immediately. Then i=1 checks the budget before the wait: if the first iteration took 0ms, the budget check is 0+30000 > 240000 false, so it waits 30s and polls. Worst case: 9 iterations with 8 waits of 30s = 240s, plus the liveHsts GET (which can take time), plus the initial fetch — total can exceed the 300s slot timeout and the lock's stale window. The liveHsts GET is memoized per probe, but the first call can be slow.
findings.why: The budget check is off by one iteration (i=0 skips it) and the liveHsts GET plus the initial fetch are not counted in the budget, so the worst case can exceed the slot timeout.
findings.fix: Check the budget before the first iteration too, and include the liveHsts GET time in the budget.
findings.twin_of: A provider wait longer than the runner's stale-lock window let a second apply break the lock mid-create
